name: Tomas Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. This conversation is confidential. Tell me what a normal day on the rail refunds line sounds like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It begins with a missed connection and somebody who has already told the story twice. I look up the fare rule, check the train record, and make the refund or explain why it cannot be made. I use an AI draft every day to organise the account, then check the fare clause myself. A fair answer is often slower than the queue timer wants.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sits behind your decisions about work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Amara works at the school library, and our two grown children have homes of their own. I earn above the usual agent rate because I cover the late refund desk. We have about eleven months of expenses saved, but the mortgage still takes a regular payment, so I would not pretend a reserve is the same as wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my desk mates the AI draft remains a filing aid, not the person who decides a passenger's refund. The fare rule and the train record still need checking. I don't see the late desk closing over a tidier note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My higher late-shift pay should stay, and Amara's library wage should too. Eleven months saved makes a missed shift manageable, although the mortgage still comes monthly. I would keep using the draft tool, as I do already, without buying a story about magic productivity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep the late refund desk and check every AI draft against the fare clause before sending a decision. I'll put a set part of each late-shift premium into our mortgage reserve. If the plateau continues into its first year, I'll keep the same checks and transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can live with a tool that saves a little typing while I still make the decision and get paid for the shift. My worry about an incorrect refusal is older than this AI question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad draft get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It can miss that a second train was cancelled and tell the passenger their first ticket still counts. A wrong refusal means a second call and a person who has spent another evening arguing. I put the train number beside the clause before I press send.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A gap in pay, a roof repair or time to look carefully if the desk changes. Our grown children should not have to bridge our mortgage. Eleven months saved is breathing room, not a reason to stop checking the account.

say: I'd call the **AI draft** a filing aid while people decide refunds.
I'd keep **fare clauses** and train records checked before sending refusals.
think: I expect **late-shift pay** and Amara's library wage to continue.
I see eleven months saved as **breathing room**, not a wage replacement.
do: Keep the **late refund desk** and check AI drafts against fare clauses and train records.
Put part of each **late-shift premium** into the mortgage reserve while paid shifts continue.
feel: **Calm** about paid work, while still careful about incorrect refusals.
S0.quote: Eleven months saved is breathing room, not a reason to stop checking the account.
fieldNote: He already uses **AI drafts daily**, so his ordinary checks are current work rather than new AI learning.
His **higher late-shift pay** and eleven-month reserve soften routine uncertainty, while the mortgage remains a fixed obligation.

steps.text: Keep late refund shifts and verify AI drafts against train records
Transfer part of each paid late-shift premium into mortgage reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the agents that automated bookings and first replies will shrink our queue, and the operator should say whose paid hours go with it. We need a human appeals desk with power to correct a wrong refusal. I would bring that demand to our union meeting rather than leave one colleague to ask alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even a good appeal worker can lose the late premium if the rota gets smaller. I am comfortable with tools, but I have never used the new exception console that scores refund disputes. I would want to understand its errors before anybody calls my experience obsolete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll join the union's group request for written cut dates, paid appeal hours and reversal authority. I'll take a paid training shift on the new AI exception console, comparing its recommendations with actual cancelled-train records and noting misses. As the slower change spreads, I'll keep the late refund shifts while they are offered and paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can act. A clever console does not pay our mortgage if the operator cuts the evening rota. I want a fair passenger decision and a paid person accountable for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your group ask the operator to publish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The numbers of paid late and appeal hours, the cut dates and who can reverse a refusal. A human appeals desk without reversal power is just another queue. We would put the request in writing and share the reply with the whole team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the new console?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a real cancelled connection and follow the console's cited fare rule back to the train record. If it skips the second cancellation, I would record that and raise it on the paid training shift. That is learning a new tool, not just using my old drafting shortcut.

say: I'd join a **union group request** for cut dates and paid appeal hours.
I'd argue for a **human appeals desk** with power to reverse wrong refusals.
think: I fear losing the **late premium** even if some appeal work remains.
I can learn the **new AI exception console**, but its errors need real case checks.
do: Join the **union request** for written cut dates, paid appeal hours and reversal authority.
Learn the **new AI exception console** on a paid shift by checking decisions against cancelled-train records.
Keep **paid late refund shifts** while the operator offers them.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced evening pay, with a clear group and training response.
S1.quote: A human appeals desk without reversal power is just another queue.
fieldNote: His **group demand** covers actual paid hours and reversal authority, not only a meeting about technology.
He commits to **new AI learning** on paid time, beyond the AI drafting he already uses daily.
The possible loss is his **late premium**, even if some complicated refunds remain.

steps.text: Join union group request for written cut dates paid appeal hours and reversal authority
Learn new AI exception console on paid shift using cancelled-train records
Keep taking paid late refund shifts while offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Amara that full thinking AI by 2028 could read the fare and train record before I finish the first call. Robots on platforms come around 2031, which gives physical passenger work a different clock. I would ask our union to demand paid notice and human appeal rights from the operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My late refund wage could end, perhaps the whole desk. Eleven months saved and Amara's pay give us a search window, but they do not turn every nearby call centre into a safe opening. I am worried about the mortgage, not looking for a heroic new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll join the union demand for written cut dates and a paid passenger appeal route. If the late desk closes in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for an advertised paid platform-assistance post only after Amara and I check its weekly hours and after-travel pay against the mortgage and essential bills. I would keep taking paid refund calls until the desk actually closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the higher wage, although I have time and people to work with. Eleven months can vanish if I treat a lower paid post as a solution before checking the weekly figures. I don't expect the union to manufacture a platform vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at the station?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help passengers with luggage or a ramp, if the station trains and pays me for those tasks. I can talk to an angry traveller, but I wouldn't pretend to know safe lifting without instruction. Hands-on robots around 2031 could reach some of that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a lower wage ever be acceptable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the written weekly hours and after-travel wage, together with Amara's actual pay, cover the mortgage and essentials. We can use a bounded part of the reserve during a genuine search, not indefinitely. I would apply first and take platform work only after signing a paid offer.

say: I'd ask the **union** for paid notice and a human appeal route.
I'd tell Amara **2028 AGI** threatens refunds before 2031 platform robots.
think: I expect the **late refund wage** could end with the desk.
I know eleven months saved and Amara's pay do not guarantee a **safe local job**.
do: Join the **union demand** for written cut dates and paid passenger appeals in 2026.
After closure, apply for **posted paid platform work** if written weekly hours and after-travel pay plus Amara's wage cover mortgage/essentials.
Keep **paid refund calls** until closure; take paid platform duties only after signed offer and safe-lifting instruction.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely loss of higher pay, while retaining a bounded search cushion.
S2.quote: I am worried about the mortgage, not looking for a heroic new title.
fieldNote: His **union demand** seeks paid notice and appeal rights for workers and passengers.
The platform application follows **desk closure** and checks written weekly hours and after-travel household coverage with Amara.
He keeps paid refund calls until closure and takes platform work only after a **signed paid offer**; robots remain a later risk.

steps.text: Join union demand for written cut dates and paid passenger appeal route
Apply after closure for posted paid platform if written weekly-hours/pay and after-travel household wages cover mortgage/essentials
Require safe-lifting instruction before accepting paid platform duties
Keep paid refunds until closure; start platform work only after signed paid offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years allows the operator and workers to try a paid passenger-assistance rota before general AI reaches refunds in 2031. It is still worth bargaining for appeal rights; passengers need somewhere to challenge a wrong automated denial. Robots around 2034 are a later limit on platform tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could try real platform work while I still have higher paid late calls. A course brochure would tell me less than one paid station shift. The station may not have enough jobs for everyone, so I cannot put a vacancy in our budget until one is posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll ask with union colleagues for one paid station trial rota open to agents, with the shift hours and lifting instruction published. If an advertised paid platform opening is offered for a trial, I'll take one paid shift and check its actual hours, travel cost and safe duties. In the first year after 2031, if refund calls close, I'll apply to a still-posted platform job only if its written weekly wage and hours, after travel and with Amara's pay, cover our mortgage and essentials; I'll start only after signing a paid offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can learn a real station shift in five years. I would rather find out now that I cannot handle a ramp than promise our mortgage to a job I have never done. The later robots make me wary of calling it permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union ask for besides a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid appeal worker with authority to correct a denied refund, and fair access to the trial shifts. There should be a written rota rather than a manager picking favourites quietly. We would bring the request back to the agents before agreeing to any change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no station job is posted in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep searching actual paid openings while using the reserve only against a written monthly budget. I would not leave the current paid desk for an unposted station promise. If the desk has already closed, the search is work, but it is not income.

I'd say **2034 robots** still limit physical platform work after 2031 AGI.
think: I can test **real platform duties** while late calls still pay.
I cannot budget an **unposted vacancy**, even with five years to prepare.
do: With union colleagues, request **fair paid trials** and paid appeals with correction authority.
Keep paid refunds; take an advertised **paid platform trial** if offered, checking safe lifting, hours and travel.
After closure, apply for **posted paid platform** if written weekly household pay/hours after travel cover mortgage/essentials; sign, otherwise search budgeted paid jobs.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test a paid route but no guaranteed vacancy.
S3.quote: A course brochure would tell me less than one paid station shift.
fieldNote: He prefers a **paid trial** with safe lifting instruction to an abstract course promise.
His group request seeks **fair trial access** plus a paid appeal worker able to reverse refusals.
A post must remain **advertised and paid** after closure, with written weekly hours and after-travel household coverage before signing.

steps.text: Request fair paid platform trials and paid appeals with correction authority through union
Keep paid refunds; take offered paid platform trial for advertised opening; check safe lifting/travel/hours
Check written weekly hours and after-travel household pay against mortgage/essentials; sign offer before starting
Apply after 2031 closure only if covered; otherwise search paid openings against written monthly reserve budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is long enough to ask what fair appeals and paid work actually look like, not just what the operator forecasts. I would be sixty-eight in 2036, and I might no longer depend on the refund desk. I won't claim that without opening our account books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our reserve is strong today, but ten years of mortgage and ordinary living can change the picture. I had planned to work through 2036 if the desk allowed; verified figures might let me retire sooner. I don't know what income or benefits will exist for us then, so I need the real figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 Amara and I will review the mortgage, savings and actual household income each year, and I will keep a portion of the late premium in the reserve while paid shifts continue. If our verified income and assets can sustain our essential bills over the years ahead, I will retire from paid work before 2036; if not, I will keep paid work as long as available. In the first year after 2036, if AGI ends remaining calls while we still need wages, I'll look at posted paid local work rather than count the children as a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened today. I have a decade and eleven months already saved, and I can make decisions with Amara. A made-up retirement date would be less comfort than a sheet of true numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an earlier departure real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would need verified continuing income and savings that cover the mortgage and essentials for the years ahead, not just a few months. I would not assume a pension payment without seeing it documented. If the numbers are short, I keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of the union in a long transition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written route for correcting automated fare refusals, with paid workers and access for people who cannot use an app. I will join the union request for that while we still have a voice at work. A public service should not become a maze because a cheap answer appears on a screen.

say: I'd ask for **paid human appeals** throughout a longer transition.
I'd say **2036 AGI** is not a retirement income plan.
think: I might bring **retirement forward** before 2036 if verified resources sustain our bills.
I cannot assume a **pension payment** or grown children's support without evidence.
do: Review **mortgage and income** yearly, saving late premium; retire before 2036 only if verified resources sustain years of essential bills.
Join the union demand for **paid human appeals** with correction authority and non-app access.
Seek **posted paid local work** after 2036 call closure only if household wages remain necessary.
feel: **Uneasy** about unknown future income, with time and assets to decide carefully.
S4.quote: A made-up retirement date would be less comfort than a sheet of true numbers.
fieldNote: He may choose **earlier retirement** only after verifying durable household coverage, without assuming any pension entitlement.
His progressive outlook continues through **paid human appeals** and access for people unable to use an app.
If 2036 calls end while wages remain necessary, he seeks **posted paid local work**, not support from grown children.

steps.text: Review actual household income and mortgage yearly; save part of paid late premium

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the refund desk and my late premium could vanish together. A union-negotiated notice date, paid appeal rights and a real platform trial would help, provided the weekly money meets our mortgage. A wage is a public promise only when someone actually puts it on the rota.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask passengers whether they can challenge an automatic refusal without an app. Some people on the late train have no working phone by the time they get home. I would like their account to count too.

headlineQuote: A wage is a public promise only when someone actually puts it on the rota.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Tomas handles rail refunds and checks daily AI drafts against fare clauses and train records.
He has **secondary schooling**, higher late-shift pay, an eleven-month reserve, a mortgage and two grown children living separately.
He brings a **union demand** for paid appeal authority and learns a new AI exception console on paid time.
Fast AGI threatens his **late premium**; slower futures give him room to test physical station work and verify retirement finances.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his late refund desk and higher paid shifts together.
whatWouldHelp: **Union-negotiated notice**, paid appeal authority and a real paid station trial would help if weekly income covers the mortgage.
